item.title: Spain to become most visited country in the world by 2040
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
France – with its patchwork landscape of quaint rural villages, glamorous seaside towns and historical cities – is an easily accessible, year-round destination, drawing visitors from around the world to its smorgasbord of culture, history and charm. So it's hardly surprising, then, that France remains the most visited country in the world. According to Atout France, the country's tourism development agency, France welcomed a record 102 million international visitors in 2025, up from 100 million in 2024, cementing its position as the world's most popular tourist destination. However, its position in the top spot may be short-lived, as according to a 2024 report entitled ‘NextGen Travelers and Destinations’, jointly conducted by Google and Deloitte, there is another country that could overtake France to become the world's most visited destination by 2040: Spain. Still the world's second most visited country, the European destination – already well-known for its family-friendly hotels, honey-hued sandy beaches and myriad eating opportunities for foodies in-the-know – welcomed a record 96.8 million international tourists in 2025, up from 93.8 million in 2024. According to the 2024 Google and Deloitte report, Spain is forecast to welcome 110 million international tourists annually by 2040, followed by France (105 million) and the United States (100 million). And it's not hard to understand why. With an average of 300 sunny days per year, the European destination is particularly popular with Brits who are able to snap up affordable airfare deals and head for some short-haul sun. During the summer months, temperatures can rise to the high 30s, and even winters here come with a healthy dose of Vitamin D. The 110 million visitor prediction would mark an increase of around 13.6 per cent compared with 2025, when a record 96.8 million international tourists visited Spain, according to the country's National Statistics Institute (INE). That's up from 93.8 million in 2024 and 85.2 million in 2023, showing just how quickly Spain's tourism industry has grown in recent years. This is already a record-breaking number for the region, sparking a swathe of new restaurants, bars and hotel openings in order to accommodate the ever-growing masses. In the first nine months of 2026, Spain welcomed more than 80.5 million international tourists, 5.2 per cent more than during the same period in 2025, according to the latest data published by the National Statistics Institute (INE). The country also set a new record for tourist spending during the period, with foreign visitors bringing in €114.38 billion, an increase of 8 per cent on the previous year, according to the INE's Tourist Expenditure Survey. For now, though, France remains in pole position as the most-visited country in the world. According to the OECD's Tourism Trends and Policies 2026 report, Germany, Belgium and the UK were France's largest sources of international visitors in 2024, while travellers from further afield continue to flock to the country. In fact, according to Atout France, overnight stays by American visitors increased by more than 10 per cent in 2025 compared with the previous year. As Hannah Free, Travel & Tourism Analyst at GlobalData, says: “Alongside Italy and Spain, France represents a significant segment of the growth in Western Europe. The country is not only popular with travellers from Europe itself — especially the UK, Germany and Belgium — but it is also popular with visitors from further afield, including China and the United States. In fact, France is one of the top Western European destinations for US travellers.” Spain, meanwhile, continues to break tourism records. With international visitor numbers continuing to climb and the country moving closer to the 110 million annual visitors forecast by Google and Deloitte in 2024, the question is no longer just whether Spain could overtake France, but how it will accommodate millions more tourists. The Spanish government's Tourism Strategy 2030, approved in October 2025, aims to address some of these challenges by promoting more sustainable tourism and encouraging visitors to explore beyond the traditional hotspots. Whether Spain will take the top spot by 2040 remains to be seen, but its popularity shows little sign of waning.

item.title: Are US Flight Schedules Returning to Normal? What Thanksgiving Travelers Need to Know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Travel chaos erupted at US airports over the weekend following a historic FAA ground stop that paused all flight takeoffs across the country for nearly five hours. The ground stop, declared by the FAA amid air traffic control issues on Friday, November 13, stranded millions of fliers nationwide, with tens of thousands of flight delays and cancellations continuing for days. Now, with the busy Thanksgiving travel period fast approaching, travelers are wondering when US air travel system will return to normal. Fortunately for travelers, both federal officials and airlines are doing everything they can to get flight schedules back on track and have airport operations running smoothly in time for the holiday rush. “Recovery to normal operations will be slow and steady,” says a November 15 statement from the FAA. “We ask for your patience as airlines work to get you to your destination.” Although the incident is frustrating, experts say that travelers shouldn’t be concerned about the safety of the air traffic control system. “While the disruption was significant, travelers should take confidence in knowing that safety remained the top priority throughout the incident,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of the US Travel Association. “Our aviation professionals deserve tremendous credit for managing the crisis and getting Americans safely back on their way." If you have Thanksgiving travel plans and you're flying out this week, here's what to know about the current state of air travel in the US. What caused the nationwide FAA ground stop? The ground stop was issued due to air traffic control equipment outages and issues with telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” says the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.” On Friday afternoon, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The company was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” says an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.” Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA says that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications issues are still under investigation. Regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a Sunday interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.” Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring. Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Freeman. “Friday's disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.” Will this impact my Thanksgiving travel plans? Air travel experts say that the ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans beginning later this week should be minimal. As of Monday afternoon, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. There were still about 2,800 flight delays within, into, or out of the US on Monday, and nearly 330 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware data. It also helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this year compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually the busiest air travel day of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying, American Airlines, the largest carrier at DFW, said its operations were returning to normal on Monday. “American is prepared to operate a largely normal schedule Monday, Nov. 16, following the FAA's nationwide ground stop,” the carrier said in a statement. "With crews and aircraft in position and favorable weather expected across our system, we are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event.” Delta has also advised its passengers traveling on Monday to continue to allow extra time at the airport for any lingering effects on flight schedules. “While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations,” the carrier said. Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight. Can I change my flight for free? Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop. However, two major carriers still have travel waivers in place. Delta is still allowing passengers scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16, to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Travelers’ new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy. American Airlines is waiving change fees for passengers booked to travel to or from one of 21 major US airports through Wednesday, November 18. Passengers can choose a new travel date through November 21, but all changes must be made by November 18. Even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class. Could a similar incident happen again? It’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages over the long run. “The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.” Airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”

item.title: What to Pack for a Stay at the Hotel Sacher, Vienna’s Grandest Grand Dame
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
This grande dame has long held the title of society hot spot: Everyone from King Charles to Grace Kelly has passed through its damask suites. In honor of its 150th anniversary, however, Hotel Sacher Vienna is celebrating its rich tradition of fostering the arts by commissioning Austrian artist Erwin Wurm to create two surreal anthropomorphic sculptures of bright pink handbags to flank its doors. Earlier this year American artist Kaws also designed a limited edition box for its famed Sacher torte cake, as did tastemaker Aerin Lauder on another occasion, adorning hers with golden flowers inspired by Viennese decorative arts. Join the festivities by channeling the aesthetics of former regular Gustave Klimt—think jewel tones and sequins that will shimmer below the chandeliers of the ruby-red Rote Bar.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Decide Which Ski Pass Is Best For Your Winter Travel Plans
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
With snow already falling in the Rockies and a strong El Niño weather pattern expected to benefit certain US mountain regions, skiers and riders are already dusting off their gear and booking their winter trips. Of course, skiing and snowboarding aren’t typically budget-friendly sports. Once you factor in meals, lodging, and transportation in addition to a lift ticket (which costs well over $300 per day at several US resorts), it’s almost worth taking out a loan to pay for a one-week family ski trip. But in recent years, the industry has moved away from one-day lift tickets in favor of multi-mountain ski passes with heavily discounted rates and additional perks, like Epic’s “Pay Over Time” or Ikon’s deals on friends and family tickets. "For those who ski or ride more than six to eight days a season, multi-mountain passes have reshaped the [ski] resort industry,” says Olivia Rowan, publisher of trade magazine Ski Area Management. “The multi-mountain pass opened up new possibilities for snow sports travel and tourism beyond your home hill. They're a great deal for an in-the-know skier or rider.” Before choosing a pass, determine your skiing goals for the season. If you’re looking to check out a handful of new resorts for a day or two each, the Indy Pass might be your best option. But if you’re hoping to spend a week at a more popular resort like Park City, the Epic or Ikon passes are the way to go. To figure out which pass is best for you and your travel plans, here's a breakdown of the major players. Best for: Individuals and families who want unlimited access to some of the world's largest and most popular ski areas When the Vail-owned Epic Pass debuted in 2008, it was the first of its kind and set the stage for the multi-mountain passes that followed in the coming years. Today, it remains one of the biggest players in the industry, offering access to over 90 resorts in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia. Pricing: The standard Epic Pass, which offers unlimited access to all its resorts, costs $1,169. But if you don’t plan to ski during holiday weeks and weekends, consider the Epic Local Pass, which excludes peak dates at certain resorts. Epic also offers a customizable pass that lets skiers choose up to 7 days across different resort tiers. The cheapest option, at $337, gives skiers 7 days at 22 resorts in the Midwest, Northeast, and Mid-Atlantic. Where to visit with the Epic Pass: - Best for the ski villages: Vail, Colorado - Best for expansive terrain: Les Trois Vallées, France Traveler-approved ski resorts near Epic Pass mountains: Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check out several uncrowded, under-the-radar ski resorts The Indy Pass, which is the antithesis of larger passes like Epic and Ikon, offers two days of skiing at each of its over 300 partner resorts across four continents. The pass partners with smaller, independently owned resorts that are typically uncrowded and have deeply rooted local vibes. This season, Indy is rolling out an upgrade that lets passholders ski up to five days at 13 resorts, starting at $199. The pass sells out quickly and is already off sale for the 2026-27 ski season, but now is the time to get on the waiting list for next season (sales sometimes reopen mid-season, too). Pricing: The Indy+ Pass, which doesn’t have blackout dates, costs $469 for adults and $299 for kids 12 and under. Where to visit with the Indy Pass: - Best for East Coast snow: Jay Peak, Vermont - Best for families: White Pass, Washington - Best for aprés: Black Mountain, New Hampshire Traveler-approved ski resorts near Indy Pass mountains: Best for: Skiers who live near one of Ikon’s premier destinations, or families with children who want to take advantage of Ikon’s discounted kids passes Like the Epic Pass, the Ikon Pass offers unlimited access to some of the world’s most popular ski resorts. The pass includes access to over 70 resorts across 13 countries, including some bigger US destinations like Jackson Hole, Deer Valley, and Aspen Snowmass. Pricing: Like Epic, Ikon offers tiered passes, with its unlimited pass starting at $1,529 (or $1,129 for young adults ages 13-22 and $499 for children ages 5-12). The base pass, which has some blackout dates, starts at $1,099 for adults over 23. Skiers and riders who want to dip their toes into the sport or who may not have time to get out much during the season should consider a personalized pass that allows two, three, or four days at partner resorts. Where to visit with the Ikon Pass: - Best for beginners: Big Bear Mountain Resort, California - Best for new terrain and amenities: Deer Valley, Utah - Best for West Coast aprés: Palisades Tahoe, California Traveler-approved ski resorts near Ikon Pass mountains: Best for: East Coast skiers and riders who mostly plan on skiing in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, or eastern Canada, or individuals looking to supplement another multi-mountain pass; It includes two mountains in Colorado and Wyoming, but they are on the smaller side. New for the 2026-27 ski season, the Snow Pass is the newest player in the game. Like Indy, the Snow Pass offers two days at each partner resort, but so far it has only 14 resorts to choose from, most of which are in the Northeast. You can buy additional days for 30% off the retail price. Snow Pass offers an alternate three-day pass—Snow Triple Play—that includes three days total at 23 partner resorts. Pricing: The Snow Pass costs $379.99, and the Snow Triple Play costs $189.99. Where to visit with the Snow Pass: - Best access from New York City: Mountain Creek, New Jersey - Best New England resort for families: Cranmore, New Hampshire - Best for challenging terrain: Whiteface, New York Traveler-approved ski resorts near Snow Pass mountains: Best for: Skiers and riders who want to check some big-name resorts off their list but aren’t looking to ski for an extended period at one ski area, or those looking to supplement another multi-mountain or season pass. The Mountain Collective Pass offers passholders two days each at its 27 resorts in the US, Canada, Japan, Europe, South America, Australia, and New Zealand. It’s a slightly more affordable alternative to the Epic and Ikon, yet it still gives skiers access to big-name resorts like Jackson Hole and Big Sky. Pricing: The Mountain Collective Pass goes for $729 for adults, $594 for teens, and $304 for kids 6-12. Skiers and riders who want to ski more than their allotted 2 days at a specific resort can purchase day tickets at half off. Where to visit with the Mountain Collective Pass: - Best for steep terrain: Jackson Hole, Wyoming - Best for deep snow: Revelstoke, British Columbia Traveler-approved ski resorts near Mountain Collective mountains:

item.title: Bagel makers, lovers and critics converged in New York for best bagel contest
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture
Bagel makers, lovers and critics converged in New York for best bagel contest The best bagel contest in New York City last weekend drew competitors from around the world, and of course lots of hometown bagel makers and critics. SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: A beloved weekend morning ritual for many people is the bagel. Sometimes just toasted with butter or cream cheese hits the spot. Sometimes you want a full-blown bacon, egg and cheese bagel sandwich. If you are a bagel lover, you might have wished you could have attended this weekend's seventh annual BagelFest in New York. Thousands of people were there, including reporter Jeff Lunden. Here's his story. JEFF LUNDEN: As a New Yorker, I appreciate a good doughy bagel. Sam Silverman, the founder of BagelFest, does too. He grew up in Massachusetts, eating bagels from Dunkin' Donuts, and loved them. But when he moved to New York... SAM SILVERMAN: And I had my very first bagel, real bagel from Ess-a-Bagel, it changed my life. LUNDEN: So much so that seven years ago, he started BagelFest, and every year they crown the best in show. He says there are four criteria - flavor, texture, appearance and aroma. SILVERMAN: It needs to be crunchy on the outside, soft and chewy on the inside. LUNDEN: That's not all. SILVERMAN: From the taste perspective, we want multi notes. We want a sufficient level of salt. And then it needs to look beautiful - golden crust, nice plump shape. LUNDEN: This year, there were 52 vendors, and every one of the attendees got a booklet to make notes on all the bagels so they could vote for their favorites. And the first vendor I saw was Steven Orr from Belfast. Northern Ireland. STEVEN ORR: So we're the first, and still the only, hand-rolled bagel shop in Northern Ireland, and the first in Ireland. We try to bring a bit of a taste of home over here, so a Irish-New York fusion. So we've got Guinness bagels. LUNDEN: And can I just say, wow. I took a Guinness bagel home with me. And yes, there were other international vendors and folks from all over the U S. New York, of course, was represented. ERICA LEVY: Whenever someone asks me what BagelFest is, I describe it as the Comic Con of bagels. LUNDEN: Erica Levy is part of the family that owns Ess-a-Bagel. They're celebrating their 50th anniversary, and they won BagelFest's lifetime achievement award a couple of years ago. LEVY: We really want to celebrate this year... UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Yeah. LEVY: ...With a win or two. Would be nice. LUNDEN: Ess-a-Bagel, which translates from Yiddish to eat a bagel, offers classic tastes. But walking around the hall, there were some pretty out-there toppings. Alex Baka from Bagizza described some Korean-inspired flavors. ALEX BAKA: This is the gochujang cream cheese with a plain bagel with pastrami. We smoked it last night. And then we have the pickled radish on the top. LUNDEN: Victoria Todorov of Sisi Bagels came from Madrid. VICTORIA TODOROV: We have the buffalo chicken, which is a vegan version, the cheesecake bagel, strawberry, crunchy and creamy. And the pizza slice, New York slice, bagel with a spicy onion on it. LUNDEN: Jackson Harris and Abigail Ellis from Brooklyn were sitting with trays filled with bagel bites and toppings, taking notes. JACKSON HARRIS: It seems like a lot of places focus a little bit more on the toppings than the actual bagel, and I find myself giving better scores to the places where the actual bagel is better. LUNDEN: At the end of the day, several awards were handed out. Among them, schmear of the year, most creative and, of course... UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: The 2026 New York BagelFest best bagel award goes to Ess-a-Bagel. (CHEERING) LUNDEN: Which for Erica Levy and her family was the schmear on top of the bagel for their 50th anniversary. For NPR News, I'm Jeff Lunden in New York. (SOUNDBITE OF TINY DESK CONCERT) GRACEYN HOLLINGSWORTH: (Singing) Hey. Baby, row the boat. Baby, row the boat. Hey, hey. Baby, row the boat. Baby, row the boat. Hey, hey. Mommy, row the boat. Mommy, row the boat. Hey, hey. Mommy, row the boat. Mommy, row the boat. Hey.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Feeling Tension in the Lower-Body After Your Latest Adventure? Do This Simple Stretch.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
I often sing the praises of the Warrior I yoga pose (a.k.a. Virabhadrasana I) to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it. In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West. The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I or Warrior I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches. The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.) Of the whole group of muscles, the iliacus and psoas are the strongest hip flexors. They are often referred to as the iliopsoas because they both follow the same path and have exactly the same action. Although they have different origins, the psoas originates on the lumbar spine, while the iliacus originates on the inner surface of the ilium, one of the large bones of the pelvis—they come together in the very back of the lower abdomen and run across the floor of the pelvis, over the outer part of the pubic bones on each side, and dive deep through the inner upper thighs to attach to the inner upper femurs. The iliopsoas is powerful partly due to its size—each psoas is nearly as big around as your wrist—and partly because its position so close to the hip joint gives it excellent leverage. It is such a strong muscle, in fact, that it can influence the tilt of your pelvis and therefore the position of your spine during your daily activities. In other words, when the iliopsoas gets very short and tight, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior (forward) tilt. This type of tilt—when the top rim of the pelvis tips forward and down and the coccyx (tailbone) lifts up—usually puts the lumbar spine into hyperextension, also known as a swayback. (A posterior or backward pelvic tilt happens when the top of the pelvis moves backward, the coccyx moves down and tucks under, and the lower back flattens.) Strong abdominals help pull the pelvis into a posterior tilt, but you might be surprised to hear that even if you have strong abdominals, a tight and strong iliopsoas muscle can win the battle and tilt your pelvis forward. A chronically hyperextended lumbar spine puts the lower back muscles in a shortened position, causing them to ache. If the only thing that relieves your lower back discomfort is to lie on your back and pull your knees to your chest (therefore flattening the curve), you might have a hyperextended lumbar spine. Hyperextension also puts a greater percentage of your upper body weight onto the small facet joints on the posterior aspect of the vertebrae instead of on the solid vertebral bodies and disks, where it’s meant to be. Enter our hero Warrior I, which can stretch the hip flexors, correct an anteriorly tilted pelvis, and help decompress your lower back. But remember to focus on practicing it with a strong posterior pelvic tilt. If you don’t, and your psoas and iliacus are tight, they will pull the lumbar spine into hyperextension, and you’ll eventually feel lower back compression and pain in the pose. Here’s how to do it. You can also look at this full guide to the Warrior I pose here. There are several ways to learn how to hold a posterior tilt, but it’s best to learn the action first before integrating it into the pose. Stand with your back to a wall, with your heels about a foot away from it and your knees slightly bent. Feel an anterior tilt by moving your frontal hip points (the two bony knobs on the front of your pelvis, each known as the ASIS, or the anterior superior iliac spine) down toward your thighs, your coccyx up the wall, and your lower back away from the wall. To move from an anterior to a posterior tilt, lift your ASIS (hip points) up away from your thighs, take your tailbone down the wall, and feel your lower back move onto or toward the wall. Now that you’re familiar with the action of a posterior tilt, here’s how to incorporate it into your Warrior I. Set up the pose with your back to a wall, right foot forward, left heel pressing into the wall. Place a strap over the upper thigh in the crease of your right hip and hold it down with one hand on each side of the thigh. Be sure to keep your chest lifted and your shoulders down. If you are in an anterior tilt, your hip points will drop down toward or even onto the belt. To counter that, bend both knees a little and strongly lift your hip points up off the strap and into a posterior tilt. With the hip points lifted, gradually straighten the left knee, pressing the heel into the floor but keeping the lift up on the hip points, in order to stretch the iliopsoas across the front of the left hip. Keep in mind that for most people, when the front knee bends more deeply, up to the ultimate goal of 90 degrees, it’s hard to hold the posterior tilt. If that’s the case for you, try coming only partway into the pose. You can deepen the iliopsoas stretch a bit more by minimizing the external rotation of the left hip. When you do this, your left knee will turn out less. The iliopsoas is an external rotator, so it will try to reduce the stretch by externally rotating as you do a posterior tilt. To lessen this, be sure to turn your left foot 6o degrees away from the wall. (In standing poses like Warrior II, you turn your foot out more, so that it’s parallel to the bottom edge of your mat.) Once you’ve done that, square your pelvis toward the wall across from you as much as you can by pressing the left inner heel down firmly, lifting the left inner knee, and using the strength of the left leg to help bring the left half of the pelvis forward. You’ll not only deepen the iliopsoas stretch, but you’ll also protect your left knee from a twisting injury. As your iliopsoas stretches and lengthens, it will pull less on your lumbar spine and pelvis, and you’ll be able to lift your lower back up out of the pelvis, thereby decompressing it and relieving discomfort. You may also notice that your posture, both standing and walking, improves, and you might enjoy a new sense of space in your hips and lower back. And you can rest assured that you’re helping prevent arthritis in your lower back. I hope I’ve made a convincing case for consistently including hip flexor stretches in your home practice. It’s especially important to work them on sedentary days and before practicing backbends—if you’re stuck in an anterior pelvic tilt, you can imagine the compression in the lower back while you do Setu Bandha Sarvangasana (Bridge Pose), Ustrasana (Camel Pose), or Urdhva Dhanurasana (Upward Bow Pose). When you consider adding Warrior I as your iliopsoas stretch, know that you’re setting the stage for a strong and healthy back in the years to come. This article originally appeared on Yoga Journal. item.title: Where could it snow in the UK this week?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Winter is well and truly on its way, and parts of the UK could be in for a snowy start to the week. With temperatures dropping across the country, the Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning for England, covering a large stretch of northern England and southern Scotland. The warning, which comes into effect at midnight on Tuesday 17 November and remains in place until 11am, could see up to 15cm of snow falling in some areas of higher ground. However, those hoping for a winter wonderland might be disappointed, as the heaviest snowfall is expected on higher ground, while lower-lying areas are more likely to experience rain. According to the Met Office, a band of rain moving northwards across the country on Monday night and Tuesday morning is expected to turn to snow as it meets colder air. The wintry conditions could cause disruption to road and rail travel, particularly in areas at higher elevations. Where could it snow in the UK this week? The yellow snow warning covers parts of the Midlands, northern England and southern Scotland, with snow mainly expected in areas at least 100 to 200 metres above sea level, although the greatest accumulations are forecast at higher elevations. In England, the warning covers parts of Derbyshire, Staffordshire, Yorkshire, the North East and the North West, including Cumbria, Lancashire and Greater Manchester. Further north, the warning extends into southern Scotland, covering the Scottish Borders, Dumfries and Galloway, Midlothian, East Ayrshire, South Ayrshire and South Lanarkshire. The Met Office expects between 1cm and 5cm of snow in places where it settles, although areas above 300 to 400 metres could see considerably more, with accumulations of between 5cm and 15cm possible. Snow falling at lower elevations is expected to be short-lived and melt relatively quickly. Strong easterly winds could make conditions particularly challenging in exposed areas, with the Met Office warning of possible localised drifting snow. Snow is expected to gradually turn back to rain during Tuesday morning. Will the snow affect travel in the UK? The Met Office has warned that snowfall could lead to longer journey times for motorists and passengers travelling by bus or train, particularly on routes crossing higher ground. Strong easterly winds could also cause localised drifting snow, while ice accumulating on infrastructure such as power lines could result in power outages or disruption to mobile phone services. Travellers planning journeys through affected areas on Tuesday morning are advised to allow extra time, check for road closures and keep an eye on public transport updates before setting off. Will it snow in the UK later this week? Although Tuesday is expected to bring the most significant snowfall covered by the current warning, unsettled weather is forecast to continue throughout the week. Conditions are expected to become sunnier and colder in northern parts of the country towards Thursday and Friday, while scattered showers are forecast in the south. Looking further ahead, the Met Office says some snow is likely in northern parts of the UK at times between Friday 20 and Sunday 29 November, although the exact locations and timing remain uncertain. item.title: Where was Below filmed? How coastal Newfoundland set the scene for Netflix's number one series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Below filmed? A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop. Despite the fictional giant squid terrorising Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project. “When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveller. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland – and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen. That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways – this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says. When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.” That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture – architecture without architects – just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.” And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9 per cent by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7 per cent. Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below. The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South – a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021 – stood in. “We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.” But to get the cosy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80 per cent of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower. When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay – it’s such an amazing phenomenon.” As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along. The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research centre where Dr Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked. While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architecture of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision – and is fantastic!” About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says. The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.” When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there. “It was quite tricky, but just stunning – really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom-built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail. The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbour was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock. Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real – but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest of Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin. While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.

item.title: UPDATE: United resolves tech issue affecting departures, expects some flight delays
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United Airlines says it has resolved the technology issue that had affected departures on Monday evening. That came after the carrier acknowledged at around 5 p.m. EST that a tech-related disruption was causing delays on some departing flights. About an hour later, United said the problem had been resolved and there was "no indication" the issue was related to a cybersecurity problem. While the disruption (original story below) ultimately was minor, it came on the heels of Friday’s FAA meltdown that had already roiled the U.S. aviation industry, causing more than 18,000 flight cancellations over a three-day stretch. More broadly, the topic of tech glitches – and speculation on what’s been causing them – has become a hot one during the past week after several high-profile issues. They’ve ranged from last week’s prolonged outage of the Outlook email platform to service interruptions at several big U.S. banks earlier Monday. This time, at least, the problem appears to have been short-lived. United Airlines is investigating a “widespread system outage” affecting departing flights, the airline said Monday. In a statement, United said it was “troubleshooting a technology issue” affecting departures on its mainline flights. The airline noted there was “no impact” to flights currently in the air. United Express flights, which are operated by regional jets, were unaffected, the Chicago-based carrier said. The message from the airline came after the airline responded to a social media post, calling the disruption a “widespread system outage.” This content is hosted by X. It was not immediately clear how significant an impact it would have on United's departure schedule for the evening. United’s apparent disruption comes on the heels of one of the most chaotic weekends for air travel in recent memory. An outage at the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday led to the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Airlines — including United — spent much of the weekend in recovery mode, which fueled some 18,000 cancellations across the industry in a three-day stretch. United’s operation had significantly rebounded by Monday, with the airline canceling fewer than two-dozen flights — less than 1% of its mainline operation, according to FlightAware. This is a developing story. Check back for additional updates.

item.title: Two Hikers Rescued from Wet Snow and Freezing Temperatures Deep in the White Mountains
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike. Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and currently partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain. While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions. Although they’d packed lights, food, and water, New Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) said the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry. NHFG said that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th. In the wake of the incident, New Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains. This incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

item.title: IDEA: Well-Traveled Women on Where They Plan to Visit in 2027
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
A bucket list item is one thing—turning it into an itinerary is another. The difference often lies in deciding that the places we dream about are worth pursuing amid limited vacation days and financial constraints. It’s a sentiment captured by avid traveler and content creator, Lucrenzia Worthington: “If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.” With 2027 in sight, we’re taking inspiration from well-traveled women who are already thinking about the possibilities of the fresh, new year ahead and the trips they hope to pull off. Spanning photographers, artisans, interior designers, rock climbers, divers, and cookbook authors, they're wanderlust is as varied as it is far-reaching. Read on for how they plan to travel next, from diving Antarctica’s crystalline waters to cooking in the fertile valleys of the Peloponnese Peninsula. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve dreamed of diving in Antarctica. Maybe it’s growing up in Bangkok’s tropical heat, but the polar regions endlessly fascinate me: the icebergs, the seals, and penguins. I’ve visited the White Continent before, but seeing it underwater is something else entirely. In 2027, I’m joining Aurora Expeditions, a pioneer in polar diving for over 20 years. Even as an experienced diver and underwater photographer, it takes serious preparation: I’m logging drysuit dives off [the coast of] Cape Town with specialized gear to get ready for one of the most extraordinary dive sites on earth.” —Pier Nirandara, travel writer, underwater photographer, and founder of Immersiv Expeditions “You know, I've been lucky enough to see some extraordinary corners of the world, yet one place keeps slipping down my list. It's always ’not the right time,’ always ’too complicated to book.’ But 2027 is the year: Lapland, in February. There are direct flights from Milan to Rovaniemi, Finland, and I would plan two nights there and two in Levi. I'm dreaming of a night in those super cool glass cabins where you fall asleep under the northern lights and endless starry skies, and booking experiences like visiting a reindeer farm, husky sledding, and snowshoe hikes through frosted pines—but also cozy up indoors by a crackling fire, with a warm blanket, and soak up the winter wonderland around me. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.” —Lucrezia Worthington, content creator and freelance journalist “I've always wanted to visit Morocco, and I think 2027 is the year. My dream is to stay in a riad in Marrakech with however many friends I can persuade to join me. I want to find tagine and wander through the [medina]. I also hope to venture out to the Atlas Mountains for a weekend.” —Ríoghnach Robinson, author of Bad Words “In 2027, I'm planning to return to Antalya, Turkey. I spent a week there this year and fell in love with the food, the people, and the climbing. I'll be based around Geyikbayırı and Çitdibi, where there are limestone crags in the hills with views out to the sea. I usually find a place to stay on Airbnb and lean on local recommendations for where to eat. One spot I'm definitely returning to is Coffee Roaster 404.” —Sasha DiGiulian, professional climber and founder of SEND Bars “Most flock to Greece for the idyllic beaches and all things Mediterranean, and while I completely understand that desire, my curiosity has landed me in the Peloponnese Peninsula, in particular the central region of Arcadia. Its fertile valleys are known for strong culinary and agricultural traditions; apples, sour cherries, slender eggplants, cheeses from mountain sheep and goats, walnuts, chestnuts, and mushroom foraging. I have been obsessing over a beautiful hotel that caught my eye: Manna, located on Mount Mainalo among hiking trails and dense forests. The mountain is also known for a very special high altitude honey cultivated from fir trees. Honestly, the honey alone is enough to get me on a plane.” —Noreen Wasti, cook, food creative, and author of Feast Your Eyes: Beautiful Recipes to Garnish, Share, and Savor A first visit to South America and a homecoming to Mauritius “In 2027, I’d love to finally visit Peru and see Machu Picchu. South America is completely new territory for me, and the landscapes, craftsmanship, and food are all calling. I’m imagining local guides, time in the Sacred Valley, and plenty of exploring. I’d also love to go home to Mauritius, but this time be a tourist. A beautiful hotel, all the food I miss, and time to enjoy the island and its lovely hospitality. Usually, my visits revolve around family and catching up. In 2027, for once, I’d like my biggest responsibility to be deciding what to have for lunch.” —Nashmita Rajiah, interior designer “I’m perpetually scouting [destinations] for In Hand’s newsletter and group trips by exploring culturally rich regions through the lens of traditional craft. I'm looking forward to an upcoming trip to the Atlas Mountains to visit the female Amazigh weavers in their homes, and learning about the by-hand process of weaving Berber rugs at the source rather than the point of sale, focusing on the culture and traditions around this generation-to-generation craft. I’m staying at Kasbah du Toubkal in Imlil, a small mountain town grounded in real Amazigh village life. It’s a trip I’ve wanted to take for years. ” —Meghan McEwen, writer and founder of group trip planner In Hand “What I look forward to most is traveling with friends and family. Mornings in the sea, a simple lunch in the hot sun. Afternoons are for slow wandering, and at night we'll cook big meals from our market finds. In 2027, my family is heading to Sicily for two weeks in shoulder season, before the [summer] tourist wave. The first half we'll explore the main island, from the salt flats of Trapani to the bone white cliffs of Scala dei Turchi on the south coast. Then Favignana in the Egadi Islands, off Sicily's west coast, will hopefully be home for a week or so. The water is crystal blue, the coves are plentiful, and you can bike around the entire island easily. Tuna is still king there, though the old canning factory has long since closed. I'm dreaming of spaghetti with bottarga. At the moment I have my eyes on Villa Zu Nillu from The Thinking Traveller, perched above its own labyrinthine Roman stone quarry, into which a beautiful pool and a Mediterranean garden have been set. And I will document it all.” —Andrea Gentl, photographer and author of Cooking with Mushrooms “After last summer’s European heatwave, we’re planning a cooler 2027 Finnish escape with my decorative arts grad school friend and her family. We always mix design with fun for the kids, so we’ll visit Helsinki’s Aalto House, the design district, and Hvitträsk museum before renting a lakeside mökki for swimming, hiking, and archipelago adventures. I want to experience the “midnight sun,” but I might regret it if the kids never sleep. Truthfully, I’m more of a lazy reptile than an outdoor adventurer, so afterward, our family of four will retreat to a less popular Italian beach for pasta, sunshine, and absolutely no obligation to do anything adventurous at all.” —Ajiri Aki, author of JOIE: A Parisian’s Guide to Celebrating The Good Life and The Joie Journal “Long the secret destination of all the chic Italians I know, the low-key vibe of Maremma [in Tuscany and Lazio] is starting to also draw an international crowd looking for relaxed summers featuring all the best of Italy—raw nature, excellent food—minus the crowds and bling. For families, the Terre di Sacra Estate is on my wish list, either “glamping” on the beach or in one of their villas. And speaking of villas, Maremma doyenne Amanda Sposito is behind one of the most beautiful private rentals, the Villa Tre Querce, in town.” —Philomena Schurer Merckoll, founder of Riad Mena and hospitality group Egypt Beyond “I would love to visit Japan. Surprisingly, I have never been to Asia before, so it feels like a whole new world waiting to be explored. As a designer working with raffia and traditional weaving techniques, I am fascinated by Japan’s appreciation for craftsmanship and handmade objects. I would love to explore Kyoto’s historic temples, meet local artisans, and learn about their weaving traditions and use of natural materials. Seeing Mount Fuji in person would also be incredible: I find so much inspiration in the colors, textures, and everyday details of a place, and I would love to bring those experiences into my designs.” —Akosua Afriyie-Kumi, founder of AAKS

item.title: 3 Dead in Plane Crash on Remote North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Authorities have not released the identities of the people aboard the plane or details about the accident (Photo: Nico De Pasquale Photography/Getty Images) Three people are dead after a plane crashed on the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park on November 15, 2026. Authorities have not released the identities of the people aboard the plane or details about the accident. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the accident, the National Park Service (NPS) wrote in a statement. According to the NPS, the Grand Canyon Regional Communications Center received a call about a missing Piper Comanche at 11:30 P.M. on November 15. Produced between 1958 and 1972, the Piper Comanche is an older single-engine, low-wing aircraft that typically seats between four and six people. The Arizona Department of Public Safety conducted an aerial search in the early morning hours of November 16 using infrared and night vision, according to the NPS. “The aircraft and debris field were located by NPS at approximately 10:15 A.M. on November 16 in the Basin area,” officials said. “There were no survivors.” The North Rim is an isolated part of the Grand Canyon that sees just about ten percent of the park’s visitors annually. It’s a rugged, higher-elevation area on the Kaibab Plateau that averages about 8,300 feet—roughly 1,000 feet higher than the South Rim. All park amenities on the North Rim are closed November through April, and the road into the park closes in December. The Arizona Department of Public Safety, Coconino County Search and Rescue, Kane County Search and Rescue, and Air Force Rescue Coordination Center participated in the search efforts. Since 1986, NPS data show 12 aircraft incidents within Grand Canyon National Park: nine crashes and three forced emergency landings. At least 21 people have died. Twenty-five people were killed in 1986 when a Grand Canyon Airlines sightseeing plane and a tour helicopter collided over the park. In 1989, ten people died when a Grand Canyon Airlines Twin Otter crashed near the Grand Canyon Airport during an attempted go-around. Most notably, in 1956, a TWA Lockheed Super Constellation and a United DC-7 collided and crashed into the Grand Canyon. All 128 passengers and personnel onboard were killed. The disaster helped spur the creation of the Federal Aviation Administration, a government agency that regulates aviation in the United States.

item.title: IDEA: Transylvania trek reveals medieval villages, ancient forests and rich living history
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
I arrived in a tiny village in Transylvania after a morning of hiking through oak and beech trees. Turning onto its only street, I greeted a sun-weathered man stepping out of a Saxon home with a traditional sleepy-eyed window. We walked and he spoke, in Romanian, with the enthusiasm of being understood. He wasn’t, but I could make out enough — “Maghiara,” “Otoman,” “Sovietic” — to know I was getting a history lesson. It was my first day on the Via Transilvanica, a long-distance trail that stretches some 1,000 miles diagonally across Romania, starting in the northeastern region of Bukovina and ending where the Danube River reaches the Serbian border. As its name suggests, most of the route lies in the central region of Transylvania, where forests and farmland meet the Carpathian Mountains. Before visiting, the region had seemed to me less of a real place and more of a universal symbol. Since Irish novelist Bram Stoker published “Dracula” in 1897, our popular consciousness has turned Transylvania into the default setting for Gothic horror. The destination has seen a recent resurgence in Hollywood, providing inspiration for Robert Eggers’ 2024 film “Nosferatu” and a backdrop for some parts of the Netflix series “Wednesday.” I was curious to see Transylvania’s true character. Because I have found that long-distance hikes tend to reveal the essence of a place, I combined a few days on the Via Transilvanica with some time in the region’s gateway cities of Cluj-Napoca and Brasov. What I discovered — beneath the storybook vistas of spired castles, hilltop citadels and pastel-colored hamlets — is a culture shaped by the influences of Huns, Saxons, Ottomans, Hapsburgs, Hungarians and, of course, post-Communist redemption. With only three days to walk and explore, I needed to find a short stretch that was easy to access without a car and packed the most sights into the least mileage. I settled on a 30-mile route at the trail’s midpoint, starting in the medieval town of Sighisoara, spending a night in the revitalized village of Cris and ending in Biertan, a terracotta-roofed village topped by a fortified church. I flew into the newly expanded airport in Cluj-Napoca, the unofficial capital of Transylvania and a quirky university city where Gothic, baroque and Soviet architecture mingle. With a sheen befitting a cosmopolitan hub recently infused with European Union funding and tech-sector growth, Cluj-Napoca flaunts a countercultural spirit that embraces its not-so-distant Communist past. Order the “Free Europe” cocktail (35 Romanian lei, or about $8) at the Soviet, and don’t miss the steampunk museum (admission, 67 lei). To reach my chosen starting point on the Via Transilvanica, I took a four-hour train ride on CFR Calatori, Romania’s main rail operator, from Cluj to the time capsule of Sighisoara. The town is known for its citadel, kept largely intact since it was constructed in the 12th century by German-speaking craftsmen and merchants known as Transylvanian Saxons. The UNESCO-designated historic center is a true living museum. Children continue to climb a 17th-century covered stairway to a schoolhouse that dates back even further. Older residents sit in parks bookended by turreted watch towers and Gothic revival churches. A medieval clock tower, from which wooden figurines for each day of the week appear via a rotating platform, remains the main point of entry. After a dinner of cumin-spiced pork at the 500-year-old restaurant at Casa Georgius Krauss (entrees between 77 and 153 lei) and a night at Boutique Hotel von Graf (from 336 lei), I set off on my first section of the trail, hiking 12 miles from the citadel to the village of Cris. The easy path took me through monumental stands of beech, across rolling meadows that rippled in the wind, along paved roads and through the village of Stejarenii, where I got my history lesson. I tracked my progress using an offline map on the app Wikiloc, though I barely needed it for navigation. A comprehensive guide created by Tasuleasa Social, the organization behind the trail, also helped. The 20,000 volunteers who built, cleared and signed the trail anticipated any potential confusion, marking trees every few dozen feet and installing stone pillars to register every kilometer. These obelisks were an unexpected highlight; all are carved by Romanian artists, lending remote stretches a human presence. Within the first few miles, I was reminded why I had brought a bear horn after seeing tracks on a muddy forest road. Between 10,000 and 13,000 brown bears reside in Romania, the largest population in Europe outside Russia. I carried bear spray as well but was told that as long as I routinely made noise — so as to not surprise them — I didn’t have to worry. The Bukovina shepherd dogs that protect grazing herds from bears are cited as the greater concern, but I encountered only a sweet Pumi dog that hiked alongside me until it lost interest. All in all, I felt comfortable as a solo hiker of average fitness with above-average backpacking experience. That the trail is largely made of existing forest roads and agrarian paths means a farm or a hamlet is never too far away. And many stretches, including mine, have little elevation change. I arrived in Cris in the late afternoon, as the sun hung low over gambrel-roofed houses with flowering gardens. The village of around 500 people is topped by a castle that was owned by the Bethlens, one of the region’s most influential families, from the 1300s until the structure was nationalized in 1949. When Count Miklos Bethlen, the son of the castle’s last nobleman, was forced to flee to Austria during the rise of communism after World War II, Cris fell to ruin. He returned in the 1960s, set up a trust to revive the village and enlisted UNESCO to lobby the government to restore the Renaissance-style castle. His wife and son have taken over Cris’ restoration since the count’s death, turning its empty cottages and manors into the hotel Bethlen Estates. I spent the night in one of four rooms in a former hay barn that now looks like a midcentury farmhouse (rooms from 1,775 lei). It’s one of four restored buildings that together contain 10 rooms and a restaurant, all of which were joined this September by a converted schoolhouse of more rooms, another restaurant, a spa and a swimming pool. The next morning, I hiked 15 miles to yet another fairy-tale village, Biertan. The overhead views of the medieval hamlet, with its imposing hilltop church circled by red-roofed homes, justified the final 100-foot climb. A visit to the church (admission, 12 lei), which for centuries was the seat of the Saxon Lutheran bishop, was less impressive. But stumbling upon what can only be described as a “marital prison,” along the church’s fortified walls, made the excursion memorable. The exhibit of two mannequins in a small room behind bars depicts an old Lutheran tradition, practiced by the Saxons, whereby married couples contemplating divorce would be locked up together to try to reconcile their differences. From Biertan, it was a 30-minute taxi ride back to Sighisoara, followed by a 3 1/2-hour train ride south to Brasov. The Gothic-spired city, ringed by the Carpathian Mountains, is the entry point for most travelers to Transylvania. It has grown even more accessible after welcoming an international airport in 2023. Compared with my last few days, Brasov felt more geared toward tourists, with stores selling Dracula merchandise and operators promoting visits to nearby Bran Castle, widely thought of — and marketed as — the inspiration for the vampire’s lair. After a night at Schuster Boarding House (from 489 lei), a new boutique hotel near the city’s medieval center, I had planned to visit the castle, which is 18 miles southwest of the city. But during a walking tour of Sighisoara, I learned the truth. According to my guide, the location of the castle and its Gothic silhouette are thought to have inspired Stoker, but the 15th-century Wallachian ruler whom Dracula was based on — Vlad Tepes, or Vlad the Impaler — never lived there. In fact, he was an enemy of the clan that occupied the castle at the time. My guide suggested skipping Bran Castle and going to the more enchanting Peles Castle instead (admission, 110 lei). I took a one-hour train ride south to the ski town of Sinaia and walked a half-hour uphill to the structure, which was a former summer residence of Romania’s first monarch, King Carol I. Its traditional neo-Renaissance exterior masks the sheer opulence within. Each of its roughly 160 rooms is a maximalist ode to something very specific. Forty types of wood etched in ornate detail fill the central atrium. Huge Murano glass chandeliers and an Italian Paonazzo marble fireplace adorn the Florentine room. Another room contains a staggering collection of 1,600 arms, as varied as executioner swords and horse armor. It was beyond anything my imagination could have conjured, more “castle” than any Arthurian legend or animated fairy tale. It was, like so much of Transylvania, better than fiction.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Rodents Keep Destroying Your Hiking Gear? Here’s How to Keep It Safe
