Source: Backpacker Magazine
One of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag. This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food. The most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier said than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp. You can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible. The bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle. I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap. Along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar. While a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay. I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh. Finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place. I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Big If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

item.title: How a New Restaurant Injected Retro “Latin Soul” Into a New-Build Space
item.description:
Source: Eater
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. How a New Restaurant Injected Retro “Latin Soul” Into a New-Build Space Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more Opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks. Founder Daniella Senior and designer Shawn Hausman (whose firm worked on iconic spaces like the Chateau Marmont and the ’80s club Area) collaborated on the project, ensuring that the space captured the same retro vibe as the menu. I especially hope their mini-private-dining room concept catches on. Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro. Daniella Senior: We wanted the space to really feel—even though it’s a new buildout—that it’s been there a long time. I’m kind of tired of the same aesthetic going around, one that’s almost too clean, too new, too matchy-matchy. I think that doesn’t, at times, help you communicate what the food is trying to communicate. For us, the food and the space work together. We wanted it to feel very Old World. We took a lot of inspiration from Vienna’s old corner cafes, which have been institutions for a while. We wanted a “We’ve been here a minute” type of feel. From our furniture to our tiles, [the Bar Nuestro team and designer Shawn Hausman] sourced a lot of vintage pieces, about 25 percent of the furniture. We have chairs that came from Austria and Italy in the ’30s and fabric with vintage patterns. When Shawn was traveling through Europe, he’d send pictures of things he found, and I sourced accent pieces—like the credenza in our garden room, vases, menu holders, a vintage phone—in local vintage shops. It’s definitely loud. And it was definitely fun to see it come together. But don’t get me wrong, there were times where I was like, “I’m not sure how these things are gonna go together.” Now I’m thrilled with the result. It seems like there are many different kinds of spaces within the one restaurant. Was that intentional? I love the feeling that, even within the same space, you’re able to get different vibes. We have a cafe side that we transition into an aperitivo room, which has all these textures and shades of blue. The paint job in there is insanity. It took over two weeks to paint this 300-square-foot space because of the level of detail. Then the main dining room is bright and feels very cozy, and there’s the garden room, which is primarily green, and it’s got stripes throughout the ceiling and the walls. And then we have the patio, which is a little more zen. Each room has a different personality, which I love. Some of the tables in the main dining room are also sectioned off like semi-private dining nooks. Can you tell me about that design decision? Even though the space is relatively large, we didn’t want it to feel that way. We wanted that feeling of coziness and warmth that you can’t get from a big open space. So we have three of these “mini private rooms”—they only seat about five people—but in them, you feel like you’re in your own world. Those were inspired by a cafe in Vienna. Also, we wanted Bar Nuestro to be for everyone, and that includes kids. I have a young child myself, and I know you can get nervous sometimes in nicer restaurants if your kids are being too loud or disruptive. These rooms allow us to give that privacy to those who want it, while you still get to be part of the action of the dining room. [A mirror trim around the space] provides continuity. It helps the guests in the mini dining booths feel more connected to the rest of the dining room, and it helps with service. Without being intrusive and having to check from a super close distance how your guests are doing, staff can see where diners are within their meal. I love how many hooks there are in the space. Restaurants never have enough hooks for purses and coats! Thank you. Being comfortable within the dining experience has a lot to do with the lighting and the music, but things like hooks aren’t often paid sufficient attention to. I come from a culture where putting a purse on a floor is a no-no, so a lot of the restaurants back home have purse chairs that they bring over. We didn’t quite have space for that, but we wanted there to be sufficient hooks so that people could relax even more. Do you have any tips for other restaurant operators about working with a designer? How do you communicate your vision effectively? We wanted a very unique design, and when I was thinking about other spaces that I really enjoyed, I realized that Shawn had been the designer. So that made it, for us, a very natural decision. From there, it’s all about being very clear about expectations. Understanding costs and having a clear budget from the start is incredibly important. Bar Nuestro opened just a few weeks ago. How has it been going so far? So far it’s going great. We’re very happy and we’ve been well received by the neighborhood. We’re excited to keep building it. Opening a restaurant is kind of like a camel’s back: There’s the first hump of opening the location itself, and then you have the second hump which is really building the community around it. A lot of people only see that first hump, but it’s a two-part thing. This second part has been challenging and rewarding. It’s like, “Now the space is set, let’s work on what our day-to-day looks like.”

item.title: The Italian bread that can last for a year
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Friselle: The ingenious Italian bread that can last for a year The first time I visited my husband's village in Salento, Puglia, he laid lunch out on a sunlight-striped tablecloth: a pile of the reddest tomatoes I had ever seen, a bowl of water and a pile of rock-hard… bagels? With the air of a man who was, at last, home, he began dunking them in the water. These peculiar bread rings, he explained excitedly, were friselle. To eat friselle, I learned, you have to first soften them in water – a ritual known locally as la sponzatura – to soften the bread while preserving its crunch. Then you pile on the toppings, which is a world of thrilling possibilities. My in-laws would squeeze the silky interior from some pomodori da pennula (hard-skinned, local tomatoes) onto the bread, then choose from jars of peppers in olive oil, capers they'd bottled themselves, wild oregano and melanzane sott'olio, shards of aubergine marinated with mint and garlic. Every Puglian household has its own way of loading its friselle. But these humble, twice-baked bread rings are more than just a simple meal. As delicious as they are ugly, they once sustained locals across the region, who prized them for their remarkable longevity and easy portability. So, when governments from the UK to Japan began urging households to stock up on emergency supplies of non-perishable food, I immediately thought of friselle. In Puglia, people have been keeping friselle in their cupboards for generations. Today, they turn to them when it's too hot to cook or when they want a quick, easy meal. Their remarkable shelf life comes down to how they're made. Baking is a family tradition for Gianfranco Parisi, whose grandfather opened a wood-fired forno (bakery) in San Pietro Vernotico, near Brindisi, in the early 20th Century. It was more than a place to bake bread: people brought their own dough and desserts to be cooked, while in winter, elderly residents gathered around the oven to warm themselves. The family baked for the whole town, including daily batches of friselle. "We used a special dough with a bit of sourdough starter, which made them more flavourful," explained Parisi, who is now retired. "We rolled out a length of dough, made it into a tarallo (ring-shaped bread), put one on top of the other and part-baked them for around 40 minutes. Then we took them out and split them with a twisted wire." The wire left the cut sides rough, allowing them to better absorb water and flavour. Once cut, the friselle would go back into the oven for a second bake of an hour and a half, driving out almost all the remaining moisture. Unlike ordinary bread, which contains enough water for mould to flourish, thoroughly dried friselle have so little available moisture that mould struggles to grow. They're also as hard as petrified stone; thorough soaking is essential if you don't want to chip a tooth. Rosaria Canoci, who twice-bakes friselle in her wood-fired bakery in the seaside village of Lendinuso, says that they will keep for a year if kept airtight and in a dark, dry place. Traditionally, the bread rings were threaded onto cords and hung up for storage, helping protect them from moisture and insects. Today, Canoci meticulously seals hers in plastic bags and keeps them on shelves. Jutting into the Mediterranean at the heel of Italy's boot, Puglia has long been a land of seafarers and farmers. With the Adriatic Sea to the east, the Ionian to the south and fertile farmland stretching inland, it was a place where people needed provisions that could withstand long journeys and days away from home. Friselle, with their remarkable shelf life, fitted the bill. Food historian Flavia Giordano, author of Puglia: A Cooking Journey Through a Land and Its Unique Ingredients, traces the tradition of sailors carrying hard bread on long voyages back nearly 2,000 years. She cities the scholar Predrag Matvejević, who wrote that Pliny the Elder described panis nauticus, a twice-baked sailors' bread, in the 1st Century CE. "This double-baked bread was essential for survival during long sea voyages," she explains, "and later became the staple food for crusaders, pilgrims, and explorers traveling through Puglian ports toward the Holy Land." But the grains used to make friselle also tell a story of Puglia's changing fortunes. Parisi remembers that in the 1960s, people didn't buy friselle with orzo (barley), as it was considered too poor. "People were emerging from poverty where they'd had to eat everything, and consequently wanted to eat better, like the rich," he says. "Wheat is softer and more refined." Today the snobbery has reversed. Barley friselle fly off the shelves, seen as a healthier, more robust alternative to the traditional durum wheat version. They're crunchier too, and definitely my favourite. Puglian bakeries remain a destination as much as a shop, although there are no longer elderly people warming themselves in winter by the oven. At popular ones, there'll be a queue in the morning for freshly baked bread. People will cycle over, leaving their bikes unlocked outside, where there is often a fruit-and-veg stall. Inside, alongside piles of focaccia and some of Puglia's more than 100 types of bread, shelves are stacked with packets of friselle. These now also come in spelt and multigrain varieties, sometimes flavoured with fennel seeds or peperoncino. And a new generation is finding inventive ways to serve them. At La Putea, a delicatessen in Lecce, chef Francesco Paladino makes "deconstructed friselle", breaking up the bread and combining it with passata before reforming it and topping with fresh tomatoes, prosciutto and artichokes. Elsewhere, smaller friselline often have spices like turmeric added to the dough; they're thinner and lighter so you can forgo the soak and simply top with olive oil and tomatoes. Although friselle are most closely associated with Puglia, they're eaten across southern Italy, sometimes in surprisingly different ways. In Sicily, for example, they're even dipped in milk for breakfast. In her cookbook Food of the Italian South, Katie Parla describes a version I'd never come across: capunata con friselle, where the bread is broken up and tossed into a salad, much like a panzanella. "There's a close parallel in Campania," she tells me, "where caponata napoletana uses softened friselle as the base for a summer dish with tomatoes, olives and other toppings." It sounds delicious to me, but when I suggested it to my Salentino husband, he looked profoundly suspicious. He would never dream of breaking up his friselle and putting them in a salad. But that's regional Italian cooking for you. For all these innovations, friselle remains a reassuringly simple food. A little water, a few tomatoes, some olive oil – and a bread baked months earlier transforms into a meal that can get you through any crisis. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.
